parole.significato: Used to make feminine forms of some masculine nouns, or to indicate the wife of a man with a certain profession; -ess
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -issa, from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa). Cf. also the doublet -esă, a neologism borrowed from French.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person singular present and third-person plural present indicatives of some -a (firs…
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -izat. Doublet of -ez. Compare also Aromanian -eadzã.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular present of some -a (first conjugation) verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -izō. Used as an infix in Romanian verb conjugations (similarly to how Spanish and Portuguese use the unrelated -ecer from Latin -escere, from -escō (as in parecer, padecer, merecer, etc). The suffix does not appear in the infinitive form of the verb in Romanian. However, t

parole.significato: Forms nouns that indicate the action or result of a verb; -ment
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -mentum, from Latin -menta.

parole.significato: Forms nouns or adjectives indicating propensity or likeness, being inclined toward, or having the quality of; can be ro…
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -āricius. Once created only nouns in older Romanian, some of which became adjectives over time.

parole.significato: to stray (often figuratively in a moral sense), derogate, deviate, divert from, digress
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin abbattere, from Latin battere.
Inherited from Late Latin ācrus, from Latin ācer (with a change in declension), from Proto-Italic *akris, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱrós (“sharp”).
Inherited from Late Latin addormīre. Compare Aromanian adurnjiri.

parole.significato: synonym of înainte (“forwards; in front of; before”)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin ab ante. Used in written language until the 16th century, though probably remained in usage in isolated regions a while longer. Replaced by the prefixed variant înainte.
Inherited from Late Latin albor, albōrem, from Latin albus. Equivalent to alb + -oare
Inherited from Late Latin appropiāre, a verb based on Latin prope (“near”). Compare Aromanian aprochiu, Megleno-Romanian prochiu.
Inherited from Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”).
Inherited from Late Latin ārsūra, from Latin ārsus. Equivalent to ars + -ură.
Inherited from Late Latin arātūra, from Latin arō. Compare Aromanian arãturã, Italian aratura, Friulian aradure, Old French areüre, Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish aradura.

Derived from the dated/regional form asemăra having undergone anti-rhoticism under the presumption that asemăra was a rhoticised variant. Inherited from Late Latin assimilāre, from similō, from Latin similis. Doublet of asimila and asambla.

parole.significato: so (in this or that manner), thus, like that, such
parole.testo: Probably from Late Latin ac sīc, or less likely *eccum sīc, in either case with paragogic /-a/ added as with some other adverbs (compare atâta < atât), the variant ași thus being the original form. Closely parallel to Aromanian ashi, Portuguese assim, Old Sicilian assì and Spanish así. Compare also
Inherited from Late Latin ascla, from Latin assula. Compare Aromanian ashclji and Albanian ashkë.
Inherited from Late Latin berbēx, berbēce, variant of Latin vervēx. Compare Aromanian birbec. For the meanings 3 and 4, compare the evolution of Spanish cabrón.
Borrowed from Late Latin blasphēmāre. Doublet of blestema, which was inherited.
Inherited from Late Latin blastēmāre (variant of blasphēmāre). Doublet of blasfema, which was borrowed from Latin. Compare Aromanian blãstimari.
Probably a Late Latin composition, from botum (compare Romanian bot) + Latin inflare (compare Romanian umfla). Compare Old Occitan boudenfla, Franco-Provençal budenfi, Catalan botunflat, botinflat.
Inherited from Late Latin branca.

Inherited from Late Latin būfus, probably of onomatopoeic origin. Cognate to Aromanian buf and Megleno-Romanian buf, as well as Spanish búho. The similar terms, also in the significantly less Slavic-contact language Aromanian, speak clearly in favor of a common etymology before the dispersal of Prot

parole.significato: owl (any bird of the order Strigiformes)
parole.testo: Diminutive of less common bufnă (“owl”) + -iță, from dialectal buf, bufă, from Late Latin būfus (“owl”). Compare Albanian buf, Spanish búho, and Sicilian buffa.

Probably from a Late Latin bombax or *bombacum, ultimately from Ancient Greek βάμβαξ (bámbax). Compare Medieval Latin bombacium (Byzantine Greek βαμβάκιον (vamvákion)), from Ancient Greek βάμβαξ (bámbax), Italian bambagia, Venetan bombàxo, bombàs, also Greek βαμβάκι (vamváki), μπαμπάκι (bampáki), Se

parole.significato: barrel, cask; contents of a barrel
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin buttis, probably of Ancient Greek origin.

parole.significato: barrel (a wood, plastic or metallic container)
parole.testo: From bute + -oi, from Late Latin buttis. Was originally an augmentative of bute, but became a synonym and largely replaced it.
Inherited from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia, from Latin battuō. Doublet of bătălie, which entered via another language.

parole.motivo_incerta: Probably; or from; nodo incerto nell'albero
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), probably of Gaulish [Term?] origin or from something further east, such as a Scythian and ultimately Proto-Iranian [Term?] origin. The Romanian word likely went through an earlier hypothetical form *căal or *caual. Com
Borrowed from Late Latin cancellārius, from Latin cancelli, from cancer.

Inherited from Late Latin capus, from Latin caput, from Proto-Italic *kaput, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *káput. Plural form capete from Latin capita. Compare the doublet șef, borrowed from French.

parole.significato: a long stick with a hook at the end that shepherds use to herd sheep
parole.testo: Probably from acăță, variant of agăța. May correspond to a verbal substantive deriving from Late Latin captiāre, but this is uncertain. Compare French chasse, Italian caccia, Portuguese caça, Spanish caza.
Inherited from Late Latin caecia, from classical Latin caecus, from Proto-Italic *kaikos (“blind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ikos (“one-eyed”). Compare Lombard scega (“fog”), scighera (“fog”).

Inherited from Late Latin cellārium, from Latin cella. Probably also used to mean cellar, basement (cognate to Aromanian tsilar (“cellar, basement”)), however was displaced by the Turkic beci before written attestation.
Inherited from Late Latin circāre, from Latin circa, circus.

parole.significato: to examine, investigate, inspect, scrutinize, search
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin circitāre, from Latin circō.
Inherited from Late Latin cīvitātem (“city”). Originally also having the sense of city; which was displaced by the Magyarism oraș. The two can been seen used interchangeably in old texts.

parole.significato: saddle girth, band, cinch, belly band
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin cingula (itself from the plural of Latin cingulum), possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *clinga, following syncopation and metathesis. Cf. Neapolitan chienga (vs. Italian cinghia).

parole.significato: to bake (to cook in an oven)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin cocere, from Latin coquere, coquō, from Proto-Italic *kʷekʷō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- (“to cook, become ripe”).
Inherited from Late Latin coxa (“thigh”), from Proto-Italic *koksā, from Proto-Indo-European *kóḱseh₂, from *koḱs- (“joint, limb”) + *-eh₂.
Inherited from Late Latin cofia, from Proto-West Germanic *kuffju. Compare French coiffe.
Borrowed from Late Latin combīnātiō or Italian combinazione. Equivalent to combina + -ție.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; Probably; perhaps
parole.significato: the prototype of beauty, in Romanian popular legends or traditional fairy tales, referring to the mythical female chara…
parole.testo: Probably from sânziană (referring to the mythical golden-haired fairy being), with the prefix co-, of uncertain origin. Possibly but less likely through a Late Latin Helena Cōnstantiāna, perhaps influenced by the Greek pronunciation *Cos(t)andiana. This may be due an association with Saint Helena, m
Inherited from Late Latin crēdentia, from Latin crēdēns, or crede + -ință.
Inherited from Late Latin crepātūra, from Latin crepō.
Inherited from Late Latin cucus or cuccus. Compare Ancient Greek κόκκυξ (kókkux), Classical Latin cuculus.
Inherited from Late Latin quomo, from Latin quōmodo.
Inherited from Late Latin conōscere, variant of Latin cognōscere.
From cunoaște + -ință, possibly corresponding to Late Latin cognōscentia, from Latin cognōscens. Compare Italian conoscenza.
Borrowed from Late Latin cuprum, contraction of Latin (aes) Cyprium (literally “brass of Cyprus”), from Ancient Greek Κύπρος (Kúpros, “Cyprus”).
Inherited from Late Latin cuppa, from Latin cūpa for the first few senses, with some senses later borrowed from Hungarian kupa and French coupe.

Inherited from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin canapa, *canapis (compare Aromanian cãnipã, Italian canapa, Dalmatian canapial (“cord”)), from Latin cannabis, from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). Doublet of canabis.
Inherited from Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre.

parole.significato: mounted, astride of, on horseback, ahorse
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin caballāris, caballārem, ultimately from Latin caballus (“horse”). Another theory suggests caballārius (cf. the old form călariu), with a change in declension. Compare Aromanian (n)cãlar, cãlari; cf. also Albanian kalëroj.
Inherited from Late Latin caballarius.
Inherited from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), derived from Latin caldus (“hot”).

From a derivative of Late Latin cardellus, from Latin carduelis, from carduus; the original (expected) descendant form in Romanian, *cărdel, was later suffixed with the ending -aș, and also changed due to a mistaken association with the unrelated căldare. Compare Italian cardello, cardellino, cardel
Inherited from Late Latin caballāricius, from Latin caballus (“horse”). By surface analysis, cal + -ăreț. Compare Aromanian cãlãrets, Albanian kalorës.
Inherited from Late Latin camisia, from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi (“shirt”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱem- (“cover, clothes”).

parole.significato: a shelter, such as a hut or shed, for goats; place where goats take their rest
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin caprāricia, from Latin capra (“goat”). By surface analysis, capră + -ăreață. Compare Aromanian cãpãrleatsã, cãpreatsã.

parole.significato: bedside, pillow, end of the bed
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin capitāneum, neutral of capitāneus, from Latin capita. Compare Aromanian cãpitãnj, cãpitinj. Doublet of căpitan.

parole.significato: head of a dead animal cut for consumption
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin capitīna, derived from Latin caput (“head”).

Inherited from Late Latin (via) carrāria, from Latin carrus. Akin to Aromanian cãrari, Spanish and Catalan carrera, Portuguese carreira, Occitan carrièra, French carrière (“career”) (hence the doublet carieră), charrière (“path, way”), Italian carriera (“career”), carraia (“road for carts or wagons”
Inherited from Late Latin cānūtus, from Latin cānus. Compare Aromanian cãnut.

From a lost hypothetical word *cată or *catŭ (from Late Latin catta (“cat”) / cattus), with the diminutive suffix -ușă added later. It was once attested in an old gloss with the now obsolete meaning 'cat' (now replaced by pisică in modern Romanian). Additionally, the original meaning is also preserv

parole.significato: laurel (evergreen shrub, of the genus Laurus)
parole.testo: Probably from Late Latin daphinus, from Ancient Greek δάφνη (dáphnē). Also possibly from Serbo-Croatian dafina; other theories suggest this word was actually borrowed from Latin or Romanian. See also the related afin.
Inherited from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō. By surface analysis, des- + coperi.

parole.significato: to take off or remove a shoe
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin discalceāre, from Latin dis- + calceō.
Inherited from Late Latin discarricāre, from carricō, from Latin carrus (“four-wheeled baggage wagon”). Compare Spanish descargar.
Borrowed from Late Latin disparere, Italian disparire, French disparaître, with conjugation based on părea.

parole.significato: lady, polite term for a woman, madam, ma'am
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin domna, shortened variant of Latin domina. Doublet of damă.

parole.significato: mister, Mr., sir, polite term for a man
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin domnus, from Latin dominus. Cognates include Aromanian domnu, Italian donno, Spanish dueño, Portuguese dono.

parole.significato: wistfulness, melancholy, nostalgia, longing; a feeling of missing someone or something
parole.testo: From Late Latin dolus (“pain, grief”), a derivative of Latin dolor (“pain”). Compare Portuguese dó (“sorrow, compassion”), Spanish duelo (“sorrow, mourning”), French deuil (“bereavement”).

parole.significato: right (referring to the direction or side)
parole.testo: From the older form dirept, derept, from Late Latin drictus or Vulgar Latin *dērēctus, from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of direct, a later borrowing.
Probably from Late Latin dulcor, dulcōrem, from Latin dulcis. Equivalent to dulce + -oare
Inherited from Late Latin [diēs] Dominica (literally “day of the Lord”). Compare Aromanian Dumãnicã.
Inherited from Late Latin dolōrōsus. Replaced by dureros, a language-internal derivation from durere.
Inherited from Late Latin eo, from Classical Latin egō̆.
Inherited from Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“face, shape”). Compare Aromanian fatsã.

Inherited from Late Latin fīliaster, fīliastrum, from Latin fīlius. Compare Dalmatian fejustro, Italian figliastro, Spanish hijastro, Friulian fiastri, Aromanian hiljeastru. By surface analysis, fiu + -astru.
Inherited from Late Latin fīcātum (“liver”), from Latin iecur fīcātum (“fig-stuffed liver”). Compare Aromanian hicat, hecat.

Inherited from Late Latin folia, from the plural of Latin folium, probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”). Cf. also the related folie and foliu, borrowed from the same Latin source.
Inherited from Late Latin frīgorōsus, from Latin frīgus. Compare French frileux.
Inherited from Late Latin frondia n pl, a collective noun derived from Classical Latin frondeus (“leafy”). Compare Aromanian frãndzã.

parole.significato: name given in the past to a person from a western European country of Latin origin, especially from France
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin francus (“Frank”). It may have been borrowed from Italian franco (“Frank”) or Greek Φράγκος (Frágkos, “Frank, Western European”), however the phonetical form indicates an older origin. Found in 17th century. Doublet of franc.

Inherited from Late Latin fontāna, from a substantivation of the adjective Latin fontānus, from fons. Developed phonologically in Romanian via assimilation from an earlier form *funtână (Attested in early 1900s Fărșerot Aromanian funtãnã). Compare to the more typical Aromanian fãntãnã, and also Sard
Derived from the regional / dated form fărinos, which is Inherited from Late Latin farīnōsus, from Latin farīna, corresponding to făină + -os. Compare Aromanian fãrinos.

parole.significato: February (second month of the Gregorian calendar)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin Febrārius, from Latin (mensis) Februārius. Doublet of februarie.
Inherited from Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.

parole.significato: January (first month of the Gregorian calendar)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin ienuārius, from Latin Iānuārius which originally gave the form *genariu, which was rhoticised in Transylvanian dialects thus rendering gerariu (from which comes gerar). Subsequently the non rhotic variety went extinct and folk etymology has analysed the word as been derived
Inherited from Late Latin grassus. Doublet of cras.
Inherited from Late Latin grunnium (“snout”), from Latin grunniō. Compare Aromanian grunj.
Uncertain. Possibly ultimately from Late Latin gamba (“leg”), from Ancient Greek κάμπη (kámpē), or an alteration of găbui, which has the same meaning.

Inherited from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin galleta (later attested in Medieval Latin), from *galla (“vessel”), possibly from Gaulish galla (“vessel”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“goblet”). Compare Aromanian gãleatã and Catalan galleda.
From Late Latin hībernum, perhaps via the plural hīberna. Compare Aromanian iarã.
Borrowed from Late Latin intellēctus (“understanding, intellect”), perfect passive participle of Latin intellegō (“understand; reason”). Doublet of înțelept, which was inherited.
Inherited from Late Latin diōsum, from Classical Latin deorsum.
From the verb judeca + -ător. May correspond to Late Latin iūdicator, jūdicator, from Latin iūdicō.
Inherited from Late Latin jūrāmentum, iūrāmentum (“oath”), from Latin iūrō. Corresponds to jura + -ământ.
Inherited from Late Latin lactem, from Latin lac. Compare Aromanian lapti.

parole.significato: connection, link, correlation, relationship of cause and effect
parole.testo: From lega + -tură or Late Latin ligātura, from Latin ligātus. Doublet of ligatură.
Inherited from Late Latin lendina, ultimately from Latin lendem. Compare Aromanian lindinã.
Most likely from Late Latin lucrāre, from Latin lucrārī. Another less likely proposed source is lūcubrāre.
Inherited from Late Latin illūi.
Inherited from Late Latin lūmināria, neuter plural of lūmināre, from Latin lūmen (“light”).
Inherited from Late Latin lucta, from Latin luctor.
Inherited from Late Latin laudatōrius, from Latin laudatōr.
Inherited from Late Latin mēla, from mēlum, from Latin mālum.
Borrowed from Late Latin mediāre, from Latin medius.

Inherited from Late Latin mentiō, mentiōnem (in the alternative sense of "lie" as opposed to "mention"); this meaning may derive from a reduction of a root *mentītiō, from Latin mentītus, past participle of mentior, and is unrelated to the original meaning of mentiō. Compare Aromanian minciunã. Comp

Inherited from Late Latin mixticius (“of mixed race”), translation of Ancient Greek σύμμεικτος (súmmeiktos, “commingled”), from Latin mixtus, past participle of misceō (“to mix”). Compare Spanish mestizo. Doublet of metis, which was borrowed from French.
Inherited from Late Latin monticellus, diminutive of Latin mons.
Inherited from Late Latin māchināre (“mill, grind”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, mill”), an early borrowing from Greek. Compare Aromanian matsin, mãtsinari, Italian macinare.
Inherited from Late Latin medullāris, from Latin medulla. Compare Aromanian mãdular.

Inherited from Late Latin manuc(u)lus, modified ultimately from Latin manipulus. The Romanian variant mănuchi, without the nasal infix, reflects the original form. Compare Aromanian mãnuclju, mãnunclju.

parole.significato: entrails, viscera, bowels, pluck, guts, intestines
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin minūtalia n pl, from Latin minūtus.
Inherited from Late Latin mēnsūrāre (“to measure”).
From nor + -os, perhaps corresponding to Late Latin nūbilōsus, from Latin nūbilus.
Inherited from Late Latin nonnus.
Inherited from Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”). Compare Aromanian oarfãn, Spanish huérfano. Largely replaced by the form orfan from Greek.
Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía, “right opinion”). By surface analysis, ortodox + -ie
Inherited from Late Latin hospitāre (or hospitor, hospitārī), from Latin hospes.
Borrowed from Late Latin parochialis, German parochial. By surface analysis, parohie + -al.
Borrowed from Late Latin parochia, German Parochie, ultimately from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía).
Substantivization of the feminine of Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Latin pār. Compare Aromanian pãreaclji. Compare also Italian parecchia, etc.
Inherited from Late Latin parētem, from Latin parietem.
Ultimately from Late Latin pergamēna and its variants.
Inherited from Late Latin petiolus, from *pediciolus, diminutive of Latin pedīculus, diminutive form of pēs (“foot”). Doublet of pețiol, a neologism later borrowed through French.
Inherited from Late Latin persica, from the feminine of persicum. Doublet of perjă.

parole.significato: orchard (land for cultivation of fruit or nut trees)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin pomētum, from Latin pomus. Compare Aromanian pumet, Italian pometo.
Inherited from Late Latin porcārius, from Latin porcus. Equivalent to porc + -ar. Compare Aromanian purcar.
Inherited from Late Latin porcāricia, from Latin porcus (“pig”). By surface analysis, porc + -ăreață. Compare Aromanian purcãreatsã.

parole.significato: payment (usually consisting of grains, cereals, and other produce) for an agricultural worker or ploughboy
parole.testo: Probably from Late Latin praebenda (“a payment”), from Latin praebendus (“which is to be proferred”). Compare Italian provenda, profenda, Old French provende. Cf. also the neological doublet prebendă.
Inherited from Late Latin praepōnere. By surface analysis, pre- + pune.
Inherited from Late Latin prīma vēra (“early spring”), derived from Latin prīmus (“first”) + vēr (“spring”). Compare Aromanian primuvearã, Albanian pranverë, Italian primavera.
Borrowed from Late Latin proba, from Latin probō; partly through the intermediate of Polish and Hungarian próba, German Probe.
Inherited from Late Latin porcella (“female piglet”), from porcellus (“piglet”), from Latin porcus (“pig”). Compare Aromanian purtseauã.
Inherited from Late Latin porcellus, diminutive of Latin porcus. Compare Aromanian purtsel.
Borrowed from Late Latin pūrgātōrium (“cleansing”). Compare to Italian and Spanish purgatorio.
Inherited from Late Latin picula, from Latin pix. Compare Italian pegola, Dalmatian pecla, Provençal pegourë.

From the form păduchi, from Late Latin peduclus < peduculus, variant of Latin pēdīculus (it was already attested to be used in a form peduclus by Petronius), diminutive of pēdis (“louse”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pezd-. Compare Aromanian piduclju, Megleno-Romanian piducľu, Istro-Romania

Inherited from Late Latin padūlem (“swamp”), from Latin palūdem via metathesis. Cognate with Albanian pyll (“forest”), which also shares the change in meaning. Compare also Italian padule. Doublet of paludă (“marsh”), an apparent borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Late Latin pāgānus. Compare Aromanian pãngãn. Doublet of pogan.
Inherited from Late Latin particella. By surface analysis, parte + -cea. Doublet of parcelă.

parole.significato: to pour out/forth, overflow, gush out, spout, flood
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Late Latin reversāre, from Latin versō, and modeled after vărsa.
Inherited from Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre. Compare Aromanian arãd.
Inherited from Late Latin rādīcīna, from Latin rādīx, rādīcis (“root”), from Proto-Italic *wrādīks, from *wréh₂ds. Cognate with Aromanian (a)rãdãtsinã, French racine, Sardinian radichina.
From the older form răpăusa, from Late Latin repausāre, from Latin pausō. Compare Aromanian (a)rãpãsedz, (a)rãpãsari, Italian riposare. See also the borrowed doublet repauza.
Inherited from Late Latin respondere, from Latin respondēre.
Inherited from Late Latin reus (“bad”), from Latin reus (“defendant, accused”). Compare Dalmatian ri (“bad”), Italian rio (“wicked”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“Slav”), from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos), which see for more. Doublet of slav and șcheau.
Inherited from Late Latin excurare, from cūrāre (“to look after”). Compare Catalan escurar, Old French escurer.
Inherited from Late Latin excurtāre, from Latin curtāre.
Inherited from Late Latin excaldāre, from Latin cal(i)dus (“hot”). Compare Aromanian ascaldu.
Inherited from Late Latin sēra, from ellipsis of Latin sēra diēs, from sērus (“late”). Compare Aromanian searã, Italian sera, Dalmatian saira, French soir, Romansh saira, Friulian sere.
Inherited from Late Latin similāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). Doublet of simula.
Inherited from Late Latin socra, from Latin socrus. Feminine counterpart to socru. Compare Aromanian soacrã.
Inherited from Late Latin socrus m, from Latin socer, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros. Compare Aromanian socru.
From substantivation of Late Latin spīnālis, from Latin spīna; cognate with Aromanian schinari, Tarantino spinale (“back”). Doublet of the borrowing spinal.
Inherited from Late Latin stab(u)lum n.
From sub- + *suoară, from Late Latin subāla, from Latin sub (“under”) + ala (“wing; armpit”); the preceding sub was added later in (early) Romanian. Compare Aromanian sumsoarã, soarã.

parole.significato: to thin, become/get thinner, make thin
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin subtīliāre, from Latin subtīlis.
From sânge + -os. From Late Latin sanguinōsus, from Latin sanguis. Compare Aromanian sãndzinos.

Inherited from Late Latin sementia, plural of sementium, neuter form derived from Latin sēmentis, itself derived from sēmen (“seed”). Among certain rural areas the singular is used for both single and plural. Compare Aromanian simintsã, Italian semenza, French semence, Portuguese semente, Spanish se

Inherited from Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from the Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), from septimus (“seventh”). Cognate with Italian settimana, French semaine and Spanish semana. Compare Aromanian siptãmãnã.
Inherited from Late Latin (in)toxicāre, from Latin toxicus. Compare Italian intossicare, Venetan intosegar, tosegar, Friulian intosseâ. Doublet of intoxica.
Borrowed from Late Latin tortūra (itself from Latin tortus) through French torture.

parole.significato: to tremble, shake, shiver, shudder, quiver
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin tremulāre, from Latin tremulus (“trembling”), from tremere (“shake, tremble”).

parole.significato: a rough fabric made out of horse or goat hair
parole.testo: Likely from Late Latin trassenna, a variant of Latin trānsenna (“net, trap”), either directly or via the mediation of Bulgarian тръсина (trăsina). See also Albanian tërsirë.
Inherited from Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus. Compare Aromanian tãrdziu.
Inherited from Late Latin tāliāre, a verb based on Latin tālea (“cutting taken from a plant”). Compare Aromanian talj, tai.
Inherited from Late Latin ūdāre, from Latin ūdus (“wet”).
Inherited from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.
Inherited from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus. Compare Aromanian vitsin.
From venin + -os. From the Late Latin adjective venēnōsus, from Latin venēnum (“poison”).
Inherited from Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis. Related to English verdure.
Inherited from Late Latin virgella, diminutive of Latin virgula, itself a diminutive of virga. Compare Aromanian virdzeauã.
Probably from Late Latin vīnāceus, from Latin vīnum.
Formed on the basis of voi, the variant first person singular of vrea (normally vreau), possibly from Late Latin voleō for Latin volō. Compare Aromanian voi. See also further information at va.

Inherited from Late Latin volēre, remodeled from Latin velle, from Proto-Italic *welō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-. The word passed through an older form *vurea/*vureare in early Romanian before reaching its current state (compare the phonetic evolution of durea). The 1st, 2nd, and 3
Inherited from Late Latin virtuōsus, from Latin virtūs. Compare the borrowed doublets virtuos and virtuoz.
Inherited from Late Latin viscōsus, from Latin viscum. Equivalent to vâsc + -os.
Inherited from Late Latin vaccāricia, from Latin vacca (“cow”). By surface analysis, vacă + -ăreață. Compare Aromanian vãcãreatsã.
Inherited from Late Latin scabia, from Latin scabiēs. Compare scabie, a borrowed doublet.
Inherited from Late Latin impālāre, from Latin pālus. Compare Aromanian mpãrari, mpar.

parole.significato: to share, apportion, assign, dole, impart
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin impartīre, impertiō, from Latin partiō. By surface analysis, în- + parte + -i.
From în + ainte (obsolete synonym), from Late Latin ab ante. Compare Aromanian nãnti.
From în + Late Latin dē retrō. Compare Italian indietro.

parole.significato: to flower (to put forth blooms), bloom
parole.testo: From în- + Late Latin flōrīre. Compare Aromanian nfluriri.
Inherited from Late Latin infocāre, a verb derived from Latin focus ("fire", originally "hearth"). By surface analysis, în- + foc + -a.
Inherited from Late Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos). Doublet of Anghel.
From an intermediate earlier form *înghiuți, from Late Latin ingluttīre, from Latin gluttiō, from gluttus. Compare Italian inghiottire.

parole.significato: to soak or moisten food (e.g. bread) by dipping in some liquid or other food
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin intingere, from Latin tingō.
Inherited from Late Latin intellectiōnem, accusative singular of intellectiō, from intellēctus, from Latin intellegō.

Inherited from Late Latin intellēctus, from Latin intellegō. Was originally also the past participle of înțelege, replaced by înțeles through analogy with other -e ending third-conjugation verbs (i.e. merge > mers, drege > dres, scrie > scris). Doublet of intelect.

Inherited from Late Latin sclavus or Sclavus, from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos, “Slav”); see there for more. Compare Aromanian shcljau, Albanian shqa. The Romanian word seems to have preserved the original ancient ethnic meaning before it took on the sense of "slave" later on, which is the mean
Either from șchiop or from Late Latin root *excloppāre, from cloppus. Compare French écloper, (éclopé).
Inherited from Late Latin testa (“skull”), from Latin testa (“brick, tile, pot”).

Either an expressive creation, an old pre-Roman Indo-European term, or from Late Latin titia or titta. Compare Italian tetta (and zizza), French tette, Portuguese teta, Spanish teta and Aromanian tsãtsã, tsetse.
